name: GLPG0492
lead: GLPG0492, also known as DT-200, is an experimental non-steroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) of the diarylhydantoin chemical class. It was designed to promote muscle growth through the androgen receptor while having weaker effects on reproductive tissues such as the prostate, and it has been investigated for muscle-wasting conditions including sarcopenia, cachexia and muscular dystrophy.[1][2]

The compound was identified through medicinal chemistry work on hydantoin-based androgen receptor ligands and was reported in a rat model to have anabolic activity on muscle that was dissociated from androgenic activity on the prostate.[1] Later studies in mice examined its effects in a muscular dystrophy model and in hindlimb immobilization.[2][3]

Published human efficacy data are not available: registered phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers have been completed, but no clinical trial in a muscle-wasting condition is listed among the sources reviewed.[4][5][6] The compound is not approved for any use. It is also one of several SARMs for which laboratory detection methods have been developed for doping control.[7][8]

paras: Like other SARMs, GLPG0492 is a ligand of the androgen receptor intended to produce anabolic effects in muscle and bone with comparatively reduced effects in reproductive tissue. Its discoverers described it as a potent partial agonist of the human androgen receptor.[1]

In rats, the original chemistry paper reported good oral bioavailability (above 50 percent).[1] Human pharmacokinetic results from the registered phase 1 studies are not summarized in the sources reviewed.[4][5][6] Researchers working on anti-doping have characterized its metabolites in vitro using equine liver preparations.[9]

GLPG0492 is the (S)-enantiomer of a 4-(hydroxymethyl)diarylhydantoin, developed by structural modification of a 4-methyl-4-(4-hydroxyphenyl)hydantoin series.[1] A comparison study examined it alongside RAD-140 and GSK2881078 in two in vitro bioassays and an in silico androgen receptor binding model.[10]

No published efficacy trials in patients were found. Three phase 1 trials in healthy volunteers are registered as completed: a first-in-human single ascending dose study begun in 2010 (28 participants), a multiple ascending dose study begun in 2011 (24 participants) and a pharmacodynamics study begun in 2012 (26 participants).[4][5][6] Results from these registrations are not summarized in the sources reviewed.

In rats whose testes had been removed, the compound increased muscle-related measures with much weaker effects on the prostate.[1] In the exercised mdx mouse model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a 4-week study and a 12-week dose-dependence study found that it increased strength, preserved running performance in exhaustion tests and reduced markers of fibrosis, with effects comparable to the steroids nandrolone and methylprednisolone used as comparators.[2] In a mouse model of hindlimb immobilization, it partially prevented muscle loss and was reported to be about as effective as testosterone propionate while sparing reproductive tissues.[3] The authors of these papers described the results as supporting further study; none of this work was in healthy humans or for cosmetic purposes.

SARMs as a class are not approved as medicines and are subject to anti-doping rules; analytical laboratories have published methods for detecting GLPG0492 and other SARMs in urine and animal blood.[7][8][11] The sources reviewed do not document specific use of GLPG0492 in looksmaxxing communities.

card.summary: Experimental non-steroidal SARM tested in mouse muscle-wasting models and phase 1 volunteer trials; no efficacy data in people.
card.note: Not an approved drug; no published human efficacy data.

quick.overview:
GLPG0492 is an experimental selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) that was developed to build muscle with less effect on the prostate and other reproductive tissue than testosterone. It has been studied for muscle-wasting conditions such as sarcopenia, cachexia and muscular dystrophy.

Research so far consists of rodent studies and three phase 1 trials in healthy volunteers. No published trial has measured whether it changes muscle or appearance in people.
quick.mechanism: It binds the androgen receptor as a partial agonist. In rodents it increased muscle-related measures and strength with reduced effects on reproductive organs compared with testosterone-type comparators.
quick.risks: Human safety data are not summarized in published sources reviewed. It is not approved for any use, and SARMs as a class are subject to anti-doping testing.
